body:
Two ways of ranking lotteries were introduced in the lecture. One orders lotteries by how many prizes they give positive probability to. The other compares the prizes each lottery is most likely to yield.

  1. a

    Determine, with care, whether each ranking obeys axiom I (independence) and axiom C (continuity).

    Answer

    No: with two or more prizes, the support-size preference fails independence. With a single prize there is only one lottery and the axiom holds trivially, which is why the condition is needed.

  2. b

    Both rankings are vulnerable to a certain kind of framing effect. Describe it.

    Answer

    It is not immune: on some finite prize set, re-describing prizes that the decision maker regards as equally good changes how he ranks two lotteries.
